utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we resume with the re-examination of our witness, I would like to tell you that we have received a motion filed by Counsel Susak, and we have decided to grant this motion and also to give the safe conduct to your new witness. However, we very much hope that this testimony will not be too long, because it will cover some ground which has already been explored and dealt with by other witnesses. So an appeal to you, Counsel, to see to it that this testimony will not be too long. I also understand that now it's almost sure that [redacted]. I think he will probably be in The Hague on Thursday so that Counsel Pavkovic will have ample opportunity to interview him, and then on Friday we will start with his testimony. Let us now move on with the re-examination of the witness. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I think the Prosecutor has not concluded his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. This was my misunderstanding. I would like to apologise. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Counsel Glumac. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness. We shall resume, and I am confident that I will be brief in my questions. Madam Witness, you explained yesterday the circumstances in which you conducted your investigations on the crime committed in Ahmici called by the prosecutor a genocide. Could you specify up to until what date you were in charge of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall the date, but I know that in late January, 1994, I submitted a memo forwarding the case to the public prosecutor for two reasons. One was the fact that I have gone through all the proposed witnesses, and the second was the fact that the witnesses have indicated some new persons, and I felt that it was my duty to advise the public prosecutor thereof so that he can decide whether he wished to submit a request for an investigation for those persons too. After that, the case was not returned to me. I continued working in the Court until the 6th of April, 1994, whereupon I became an attorney, a lawyer. I know that a colleague of mine continued working on this case, but I never expressed any interest in the case. I merely was aware of the fact that he was still working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The fact that the work that you did at the end of January 1994, when you submitted to the prosecutor the statements of witnesses that were gathered by you, I mean, what was the significance of this? Could one consider that the communication to the prosecutor established the fact that witnesses, according to you, were reliable in the statements they made of what they had lived and experienced?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a presumption, when one works at the court, that the witness is speaking the truth. Before a witness starts testifying, he is cautioned that he has to speak the truth and that he must omit nothing and that any omission would also be considered as false testimony, but whether a witness indeed did speak the truth cannot be concluded definitely on the basis of the record of the interview. Neither the prosecutor nor the judge, until the very end of the trial, at which all the evidence is presented individually and in relation to each other, are taken into account, and then on the basis of all those individual statements, the trial chamber decides what is the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about this very young girl you heard on the 17th of December, 1993. I'm not going to say her name, and I would like you not to say, because this is an open session. You heard on the 17th of December, 1993, in your office, a young girl who came to testify about the circumstances revolving around the death of her father, circumstances in which her house was destroyed and her family expelled. This young girl was then 13 years old. It just so happened that five years later she was heard here as a witness, and I think that she answered the questions by Counsel Radovic, and it turns out that she does not recall meeting you, and she does not recognise the signature which is on the minutes of the alleged statement that she made. So I would like you to help us understand why this young girl had no recollection of that hearing with you and why she did not recognise her signature. When you summoned that witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Radovic? I imagine there is an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. How can this witness know why the previous witness did not remember her interview with the public prosecutor? It is for her to know. This witness cannot know what was going on in the head of another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor Terrier, I think that this objection is well-founded. Indeed, it would be very difficult for the witness to establish why --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, of course I want to specify my question. I did not intend to present it that way. I just meant that the witness could help us understand the problem that we are facing by answering very precise questions as to what happened then. Indeed, I do understand the objection by Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam Witness, when you summoned that young girl, you got her name, you found her name; what are the circumstances which led you to call upon her, if you remember this?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I need an answer from the court. In fact, I will have to give you a wider explanation. Two of the witnesses that I heard, I heard them outside of the court premises. Since we could not locate the witnesses, and since we presumed that they were in refugee camps, I heard that a large number of witnesses was located in a camp some 15 kilometres away from Zenica. I asked the people who worked in an organisation called the Norwegian Peoples Help to drive me in their all-terrain vehicle to the camp. They were unable to bring the witnesses to me, to the town, because they did not have enough fuel either, and they did not know whether they would able to bring them back to the camp the same day, and they didn't have any accommodation for them in the town. In order to minimise the expenses of this organisation, I was entitled to go in the field, and I went to this camp with our typist and a typing machine. It was a mechanical one, not an electric one. I found only two persons in that camp, however. Since I saw that the record of the interview of that young girl was typed on a mechanical typing machine, I assumed it was the girl that I located in the camp. It is true that I did work using a mechanical typewriter because there were times when we did not have electricity in the courtroom either. But most of the time we did have electricity in the courtroom. Most of the electricity went to the hospitals and to the various state authorities. On that day, when I was at the refugee camp, I remember that I interviewed an elderly person and a young person. If it says that I questioned only two female persons on the 17th of December, 1993, and if both of these records were typed on a mechanical typewriter, and if both have the same recording clerk, Jusufovic Emira, then I conclude that I interviewed this young girl in the refugee camp. The camp manager gave me the names from the list of the names of all the people located in the camp. I'm telling you all this on the basis of the assumption that there are no other records typed on a mechanical typewriter and under the assumption that there are only two records made on the 17th of December, 1993. I don't recall with any certainty whether it was this girl that was questioned at the camp or whether she was questioned at the court, but I do remember that she was interviewed. I remember when she told me that their father told them to go down to the basement through an entrance that was located within the house, and I remember when she said that she tried to put out the fire that was set to the screens. At that time, I found it rather unusual to hear a story being told in such great detail, but I do remember all this. The witnesses did not have proper identification documents, they had left them behind in the village, so they mostly had temporary certificates of their identity issued to them by a service in Zenica. That was the war presidency of the Vitez municipality which was temporarily located in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Prosecutor Terrier, may I ask a question: Madam, you have brought your notes with you. If I understand what you said yesterday, you said that you had taken a number of notes, yesterday. Did you consult your notes, or could you consult them, and maybe extract major information from them?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those records on the interviews with witnesses, after I dictated them to be typed, I destroyed them, those notes, so I do not have the notes. And since I left the court, and since it is not usual to take any official documents with you when you stop working at the court, I did not take anything with me. I only took a notebook containing my personal notes with just a few of the names of the witnesses I interviewed, in pencil, since we did not have enough ballpoint pens. We did have some ballpoint pens, but they had gone bad, they did not work any more, so we kept what little we had to sign important documents and records with them. I have only some pages from my personal notebook where I noted down that on the 16th of December, I planned to have before me six witnesses. That was a plan for six witnesses, but I knew that I would be lucky if I had two appear before me because the postal service did not function. I summoned a larger number of them in order to make sure that I had at least one or two of the witnesses actually appear. It is also noted here for the 22nd of December, that was a Wednesday, I also noted down that I intended to interview, in other words, that I summoned five witnesses. There is another note for the 20th of December, Monday, when I was engaged in something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I do not think it's necessary to continue. If I understand what you're saying, you have not noted particular comments or information regarding the day we're interested in when you went to that camp in order to interview those two people. I would like to apologise. Please carry on, Prosecutor Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, if I refer to the minutes established on the 17th of December, 1993 referring to the hearing of this very young girl, could you, if you consulted those minutes, would you be able to say whether it was established in the refugee camp that you mentioned or in an office in the Tribunal? Would it be written on it?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The record was made right there with the witness present. So if I was at the refugee camp with those two witnesses, then it was done right there, and if I had interviewed them at the court, then it was done at the court. It is not indicated in the record that it was done at the camp, since it was considered to be done before the court regardless of the actual premises where it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So whether the record actually happened at the camp, at the refugee camp, or in the Tribunal, did you have with you a distinctive sign of the fact that you were a judge? For instance, did you wear a robe?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. There is no official uniform for a judge in the court, not even today, but I introduced myself, and I met some people I knew from Zepce. They all saw the camp manager who came every morning and left every afternoon to bring them food and so forth. They saw somebody else, an official who came with them. I was given an office in the camp where I was able to conduct my business. I also had with me the typewriter and the case file, so there was no doubt about the fact that I was there as an official of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But we are talking about a very young teenager, aged 13. In Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, did children in schools receive lessons in civic education on how the government runs, on parliament, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The children did not have such courses in our educational system. This is something that is being introduced right now. At the time, there was a complete disruption of the schooling system. In 1993, children sometimes did not have school for a whole month. It was done for their safety. The schools would not be open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This very young girl or very young teenager who you heard on the 17th of December, 1993, do you think that she previously had had to tell her story to several other people?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like you to disallow such questions because he's trying to see what the witness was thinking or doing before giving the statement. It's mere speculation on the part of this witness of what another witness was doing or thinking. This witness was heard before the court, and she said that she gave only a statement to the journalist, Mr. Osario, so the Prosecutor should not be allowed to ask such questions, and it doesn't tally with what the witness said during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I don't agree at all, Madam. I think that the Prosecutor asked a very specific question, i.e., if the witness knew whether the girl had already been asked, she can answer "Yes" or "No." So I think that the question is relevant. The question is, did you know, Madam, whether this young girl who testified before you had already talked about those events to other people? If you do not know, then answer "No." Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tell you that the Prosecutor did not ask the question in this manner. He did not ask whether the witness knew. He asked what the witness thought, whether another witness gave statements to other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There may be a problem in the translation. I followed the question in French, and I think the question raised by Prosecutor Terrier was the way that I understood it. Over to you, Prosecutor Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question, Madam Witness. Are you informed of the fact that this very young witness you heard on the 17th of December, 1993, maybe in this refugee camp, had previously already given interviews or already explained her story to people other than you?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not ask this girl whether she had given any official statements to other persons, including journalists, so I can say that I do not know that. But I am sure that all the witnesses from the village of Ahmici had told their stories to each other innumerable times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know whether those witnesses in Ahmici, before talking to an investigating judge, had told their stories to officials, whether in the police, the social services, or other non-official persons?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that the witnesses, in addition to the Ministry of the Interior, in other words, to the police, where they were questioned for the purposes of issuing a criminal report, I know that they were summoned to a special centre for Bosniak studies where information was obtained from them. Now, I heard that this organisation is labelled "AID." It was not AID. It was an institution that was established for scientific and historical reasons. It was designed to collect information for the purposes of historical research.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection, Madam, that this very young witness, we're still talking about the witness you heard on the 17th of December, 1993, aged 13, do you have a recollection of whether she was accompanied by an adult, possibly a member of her family?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have to say again that we have two versions here. If this is the girl who I interviewed in the camp, she told me that her mother was not there, that her mother was somewhere else. I found that strange, that this girl and her mother did not live together. But if this is some other girl who I questioned at the court, then I do not remember who accompanied her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, Madam, in your capacity as an investigating judge, when you question a witness and the witness is very young, 13 years old, do you hear that witness alone or do you hear that witness accompanied with a relative or a parent?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I interviewed two or three minors. I remember a boy. He was brought in by his sister or the mother. I'm not sure about the mother, but I do know that his sister was there. At any rate, I treated them with great care, as if they were my children. I explained to them very slowly that they had been summoned, and if they felt that they wanted to testify and that they could testify, that they could do so, but if they did not feel that way, that they were not obliged to tell me anything. In the course of that conversation, I concluded that they were able to give testimony and to understand the right that they had not to testify, as it is expressed in the law. I took some time to explain all of this to them, and I tried not to cause any fear in them or any impression that they had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. When, as an investigating judge, you interview a very young witness, particularly when it comes to children aged 13, you try to establish between you and that witness a relationship of trust. You try to act as if you were a relative, you do not seek to establish any distance between the witness and yourself, and you do not want to sound authoritative. You want it to be as simple and as close as possible.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time, I was aware of the fact that I was a judge and that I had to act officially. I never forgot the fact that I was there as a representative of the court and that I had a witness before me, but with those witnesses, I was not as stern and as official as I would be with adults.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If a third party, a parent, had accompanied that very young witness, would that be included in the report?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it would not be included in the report. The witnesses are only summoned through their representatives if they're minors, but they gave their statements on their own. That person representing their interest would not be there present during the interview, in the same room, so that it would not be noted in the record the names of persons who were sitting outside in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. So this means that, by no means, a parent was a part of that interview or assisted in this interview?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. All of them, they were there alone, regardless of the fact that they were adults or minors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you systematically would issue a warning to the witness that the witness had to speak the truth. Does that mean that there has to be a formal oath to be taken?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there was no formal oath or solemn declaration or anything like that. It was merely a caution issued on my part verbally. At the time when I told them that, I was at my sternest and my most official. I left the impression that I was there on behalf of the court and that the witness must understand that he had to act that way. I always stressed the part that false testimony is a criminal offence and that it can be punished with imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is this caution worded in a particular way when addressed to a young child?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It's worded in the same way. Everything is the same except that you have to establish that the witness, considering the witness's age and maturity, is able to understand the caution that he or she need not testify and can refuse to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, can a child be punished by a prison term in the case of false testimony?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the end of the hearing, is the witness, and I'm always referring to a 13-year-old, is the witness supposed to reread the minutes or does someone read the statement, the registrar, for instance, or yourself?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The child is given the statement to read and to sign. It is I who hands this over. In our building, the rooms are arranged in such a way that we sit in a small room, about 12 square metres, where the witness, the court clerk, and I, as the investigating judge, sit. Everything takes place there. The registrar is not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If one, Madam, refers to your recollection of the child you heard at the refugee camp, do you remember that this child had reread, with attention, the record, may have asked questions, may have made comments, or any particular event intending to prove that the child had actually understood what she had been given to reread?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the case of every witness, I had a lot of time at my disposal. No one left my office in a hurry. So all of them looked at me and listened to me very carefully as I was dictating the record. One could almost say that they were dictating it together with me, because whenever I came to an important word, at every name, even though I had already heard the name, even though I had noted it down in pencil on a piece of paper, before it was entered into the typewritten record, I always asked again, "Did I hear you well? Is that what should be put in the record?" As regards this particular interview and this little girl and the part of our encounter where she was reading and signing the record of the interview, I don't remember those details specifically. But I do remember a little girl who talked about her father saying, "Go downstairs." I remember the story about the screens and about the shoes which she managed to take. I have to say that I entered into the record that the little girl said that her father had had a rifle. If I had been subjective or in favour of that party, I would not have entered those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In your recollection of the witness you have just mentioned, what was the frame of mind of that witness when you first met her?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: She appeared quite calm. It was the mothers who cried, and elderly people, who wept more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do witnesses receive a copy of the record?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, none of the witnesses receive a copy. It's not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A few moments, Mr. President. Thank you very much, Madam Witness. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor Terrier. I now give the floor to Madam Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Ajanovic. Just a few questions. You said that you do not remember the particular interview with this particular witness. You can remember the content of the statement, but you don't remember the course of the interview itself. You said that it was possible that this was done at the court or at the refugee camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I have looked at the record, and the story about the screens brought back the memories that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As regards the person you say was young and was interviewed in the camp, you said that you remember that this person was there without her mother and that you found this rather unusual; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and the record helped me to recollect that a young person in the camp told me that her mother wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And where was the mother? They were completely separated?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The mother was in a different camp, in another place?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: She said that her mother had gone somewhere, and she didn't explain further. I didn't want to question her about it, because I had the impression that it would upset her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you recall that her mother was not living with her?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what she told me, that her mother wasn't there and that she had gone somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To clarify this further, had she gone there only that day, or that she wasn't living there?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This little girl, I had the impression, avoided giving me a full explanation. She said, "My mother is not here. She has gone away. She has gone to visit friends." Something like that. But I had the impression she didn't want to talk about it further, and I didn't want to question her. I thought it was not material for the purpose for which I was questioning her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I talked to you before your testimony --

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: -- and you said that you recall a young person and an elderly person from the camp?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With respect to the young person, you said you remembered her only because she was there without her mother, that she was living there without her mother?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how important this conversation is and whether I actually said she was living without her mother, but I say now that I remember that she said to me, "My mother isn't here, she has gone away," and I had the impression that she was not living with her mother, but I did not question her about it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said that you had, during your interview with that person, you had to decide whether this person was mature enough to understand her right not to testify if she didn't want to, and you concluded that she was mature enough; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did conclude that, and considering what she said in the further course of the interview, she seemed to talk in the same way as other people. Her testimony did not strike me as unusual in any way. The only details I remember is that she was trying to put out a fire, that some screens were on fire, and that she found this important enough to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you say whether you understood on that occasion, when you were assessing her abilities, that she was mature enough to understand the meaning of testifying before a court? Not only her right not to testify, but the fact that she was actually testifying before a court?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I interviewed those witnesses, I knew that their testimony is not the only evidence and that they would be questioned again at the trial, so no investigating judge is the last one to decide about whether the testimony is credible. It is testimony, but the testimony before an investigating judge cannot be the only basis for reaching this conclusion. It's the entire procedure that is important. I have to say that those children gave me the impression that they were mature enough to know what they are saying and why they are saying it, and I didn't -- or rather I was not trained as a psychologist or a pedagogue, so I cannot be an expert on these matters, and I cannot fully say that in the sense that an expert would say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me just put one question to you, since you did take a witness statement from that witness: Did you feel that she understood she was testifying before a court?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understood that, because I told her who I was, and she talked very calmly, she talked in a very ordered way, in sequence. She saw that I was an official person, that I was carrying papers, files, and there was no reason for her not to understand this, especially because children in Bosnia grew up rather faster in the wartime period than other children do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court whether in our system an oath is usually taken?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A witness can take an oath if required to do so by the court, but in most cases this is not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In your 15 or 16 years of experience as a judge, and then during your practice as an attorney, did you ever require that an oath be taken by a witness, or were you present when this was done?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether, regardless of the fact whether the interview took place in the refugee camp or at the court, was the procedure the same?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the procedure was the same. In the camp, I always asked for an official room, we were in that room alone in the same way as we would be in the court, the three of us. I explained everything: Why I was there, what my task was, what I wanted from them. I cautioned them that they had to tell truth, and then I said, "You can tell me what happened to you, everything you saw." I then took notes, dictated it into the typewriter, and that's how I conducted the whole interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you remember whether the camp had a name?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether the camp had a special name, but it was in a village called Arnauti, near Zenica. In that camp, there were mostly refugees from Zepce, and I found only those two persons there from Ahmici. There were people from other villages, but I didn't ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All right. That was supposed to be my next question, whether these two persons you found there were the only persons from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just one more question, please: Can you remember whether that person told you that she had made statements to other official bodies?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The girl? I don't remember whether the girl said that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you said when you answered the questions of you by the prosecutor that you were sure that the victims, the people from Ahmici, surely told their tales to each other numerous times after their experiences. What made you think so?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was like this. The villagers from the village of Ahmici and the people from Vitez organised for themselves a wartime presidency of the Vitez municipality in Zenica. Then they organised a special Ahmici society. It was not just an association of all the people from Vitez municipality, but an association specifically of people from Ahmici, where they gathered. I know that people from other villages had similar associations, who were staying in Zenica, Busovaca, Gacice, Kozarac, Gorazde, and there were people from Srebrenica and various other places, and that's why I'm convinced, since they found it necessary to organise their own association, where they could meet, and since in those places they received humanitarian aid from various organisations, I'm sure that they kept repeating their stories, telling them over and over again. The women had a special organisation, which still exists, called "Medica," for psychological support and treatment and the resocialisation of these women, and in those places they always told their stories, complained, and they do that today, and they try to establish the truth among themselves. I lived there, and as a citizen, of course I noticed this in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question: In the legal system, based on the valid law on criminal procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina, do the lawyers have the right to see what is in the file, in the case file?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They have the right to see what is in the investigating case file after the accused has been examined. They also have the right to be present at the first interview with the accused. After that, a decision on conducting an investigation is issued, and after that the attorneys have the right to inspect the file. In this case, there was no interview of the accused, and this is provided for by the law because an investigation may be opened up without an interview with the accused when the case is urgent and the investigation cannot be postponed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Another question: Do you know, or were you at any stage of the investigation attempting to determine where the accused were located, or to interview them, since you said that you had continued your work after the Washington Agreement had been signed in April 1994?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the Washington Agreement was signed, I did not go on working. I felt this as a kind of rebirth, when that agreement was signed, and I left the court on the 6th of April, 1994, to become an attorney, so I was unable to influence the summoning of the persons being investigated after that date, and up to that date -- or it may have been the 28th of March, as far as I remember, that's when the agreement was signed, but I find it easier to remember that it around the 1st of April -- up to that date, it was not possible in any way either to go there or to send a summons there. There was no communication. It was only UNPROFOR forces that could go there, and even they gave each other passes and signals. There were two armies confronting one another there, and it was impossible to establish anything. It was impossible to send a summons and expect someone to turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Since the investigation in that case had not been concluded at the time that you left, but it went on, do you have any information whether the investigating judge that continued interviewing the witnesses, whether he attempted to issue a summons to the accused?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no information about that, but -- I assume no, but I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Ajanovic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic? No questions? Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three brief questions, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether this investigation case would be considered as a major case at the court at that time?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course. Of course it can be considered an important case, but there were other similar cases before the court at that time. There were similar events in Vares, Donji Vakuf, Kozarac, and I interviewed witnesses in connection with Kozarac and the Keraterm and Manjaca camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the practice at the courts whereby such important cases would be assigned to the best judges?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no categorisation at the court of the best, medium, and the worst judges. That would have been highly insulting, to establish such categories, even though we are all aware of who has more experience and who has less experience. I am fully aware of the fact that I was given a job for which I had no experience, and regardless of your question, I do not feel insulted. I have to tell you that at my court, I was considered to be skilful, able, and energetic. However, at the court, many people left, many elderly judges dealing in criminal cases had left Zenica, so that I and people like me were left to carry on the work of the court, and there were no better judges available. Well, you said yourself there was a colleague, a senior judge who had had 30 years of experience doing only that kind of work, but she was in charge, and the questioning of witnesses was considered to be an operative task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, the very fact that such an important case was assigned to you speaks to the fact that you were a highly esteemed judge at the time.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Every job in the court was esteemed, and every kind of case had its own importance, and we never said that someone was doing a more important job and someone else a less important job. Civil lawsuits also required a lot of knowledge, concentration, just as criminal cases did. But in criminal cases, the practice is that when a new judge starts dealing in criminal cases, he begins as an investigating judge, and then after a few months he can be given cases where he will be in charge of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, I understand your modesty, and thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Counsel Pavkovic? We have no questions from the Court, from the bench. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Mrs. Ajanovic, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. We are most grateful to you. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank you for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will now move on to our next witness. I assume this is the first witness called by Counsel Krajina? Is it so? While we are waiting for the witness, let me tell you that we have decided to call Mrs. Dragica Krizanac, the lady -- assuming that we are able to trace her -- to call her on Tuesday, the 25th of May, at 9 a.m., on the assumption, as I say, that the Victims and Witnesses Unit is able to contact her. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You asked us to present our motions verbally to the Court, and I am doing that. We have this record on the interview of Witness H, which is part of the court record. In the record, it is indicated where the witness resided at the time when she gave her statement to the investigating judge. That portion of the record has been blacked out so that it is impossible for us to see what the residence is. We would like the Court to order the Prosecutor to deliver to us a copy of this record without this portion being blacked out because, as far as we understand, it is not of great importance at this time, yet it would be important for us to be able to ascertain where this witness resided at the time when she gave her statement to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall check, but the copy of the record from the hearing of that witness referred to by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, on the copy that I here, it has the same places blacked out, so I shall check. But I am not sure that we have an original or a version which does not have such places blacked out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Who would then have the original without the places being blacked out?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, on the English translation of the record, it seems that under item number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, a more simple solution, Mr. President. We can submit to the Defence a copy that has no places that have been redacted. I just found that we have such copies. We will do that in the afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any further requests or motions? If not, then we can turn to the next witness. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This is a technical issue, not a material issue. Yesterday, you gave us the schedule of our hearings, and some of us fail to understand when our hearings would resume. Some people think that it's on the 21st; some people think it's on the 26; some people think it's on the 31st of May. So could you please make it clear to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. In May, we will resume on the 25th, which is a Tuesday, because the 24th is a holiday; it's Wit Maandag. So we will resume our hearings on the 25th of May at 9.00, and we will go on until the 4th of June. I hope the witness can be brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ilic. I should call you President Ilic. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ilic.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please give us your full name and say a few words about yourself?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: My name is Vjenceslav Ilic. I live and work in Sarajevo. I'm a judge of the supreme court. I have a four-year mandate from 1996 to the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We are allowed to ask that. Can you now please tell us something about your current job?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I am the President of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you outline briefly your professional experience, how many years you have worked in the judiciary and what kinds of jobs?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: I have been in the judiciary for over 26 years, and I have worked on various tasks. In 1972, I became a judge in Sarajevo at the district court. It's not the cantonal court. Then from 1987 to 1992, I was the president of that court. After that, I was the public prosecutor for six or seven years. Then I became a judge of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the previous court. Now I'm in the supreme court again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ilic, you have been summoned here to tell us something about the judicial practice in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as regards the criminal offences, war crimes, about the persecution of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, I already told you that, as a court, with all due respect, we are not interested in particular -- otherwise, President Ilic will have to cover a huge ground. You said that he would simply comment on the two judgements we have received which deal with the persecution of civilians. If you could narrow down and specify your question, I would be most grateful to you. Let us not embark upon a description of the legislation and judicial practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina on war crimes or crime against humanities. It may be of some relevance to us at the stage of sentencing, if any, if we reach that stage, but otherwise it's of no great importance to us because, as you know, we apply our Statute and customary international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, in asking my questions, I will respect fully your request, both the one that you made earlier and what you just repeated. I wanted to adhere to those instructions, and I do not believe that we will go beyond the boundaries set by you right now. However, we have always intended, bearing in mind the fact that at the very beginning of this trial, the Chamber asked the parties to give some of our views on the matter of the persecution. Since our views coincide fully with the views expressed by the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is why we wanted to present this witness because we thought that his words would be useful. I will start from these two judgements and their commentaries. I would now like the Trial Chamber and the parties, as well as the witness, to be given the first instance judgement, number K-81/96 of the 6th of March, 1997. That is the first instance decision. We have a sufficient number of copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, as I say, sorry, Counsel Krajina, I'm really grateful to you for trying to comply with our requests, but even in the case of these two cases, as I said, we have read the English version of the two cases; therefore, we do understand what is meant by the two courts, how they went about this particular item of persecution, and there is some interest in understanding what is stated there. I wonder whether the witness could confine himself as to giving the gist, only the gist of what is said here. Because, as I say, we do understand. As I say, we are not bound by these cases. We are not bound by the notion of persecution laid down in any legislation, any piece of legislation or case law of the former Yugoslavia. We apply customary international law and our Statute. Thank you. I hope you will not take it amiss if I make all these remarks, but the purpose is just, as I say, to try to narrow down as much as possible the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. President, that this testimony will not take long, but as regards the remarks that you have made, I would like to add something. We, as the Defence counsel, and I do think that we're all in a similar situation, especially as regards count 1 of the indictment with which our client has been charged, we wanted to use these two judgements and views expressed by the supreme court and the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina in general to illustrate to the Court the fact that in the country where our client is from, and he has the citizenship of that state, that it is necessary to determine the actual act and also the mens rea or the intent if the accused is to be found guilty of the crimes he has been charged with. I have to say that the indictment that we are now trying does not contain specific acts in count 1. What are the acts that he is charged with under count 1? Throughout this trial, we have been in a situation in which we were unable to ascertain what our client has to defend himself against as regards count 1, and that's why we tried to present to the Court our view regarding the necessary elements to be proven if the accused is to be found guilty of the crimes he has been charged with. Since this is our view, the view of the Defence counsel, and since it coincides with the views expressed by the courts and the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was our intention to present the views of the supreme court to the Trial Chamber because they're identical to our own views. I hope, once again, that I will not take up much time, especially bearing in mind that we, as the Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic, have never attempted to complicate the matter, nor did we ask questions which were superfluous. I will try to make this testimony as brief as possible, since we do have this man here. He travelled maybe 2.000 miles to be here and to testify at this trial. But if we were to follow your suggestion strictly, then I think we would have to conclude his testimony right now because I would have no questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D31/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, please, have a look at this judgement of the High Court in Sarajevo. You have been supplied with this copy before, and you have it now here before you. We can see from this judgement that the accused, I would prefer not to have his name mentioned, has been acquitted of two charges that were listed in the indictment, two counts. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And the judgement also indicates that the basis for the acquittal is Article 350 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. Could you please tell us very briefly what is the gist of Article 350?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: There are three items there. The first is that it's not a crime; the second is that there are certain circumstances which, if they obtain, there is no responsibility; the third is that there is no evidence that the crime has been committed. This means, in practice, that after the presentation of the evidence before the court, after considering all this evidence, the court came to the conclusion that the presumption of innocence is as it is and that there is no evidence on the basis of which the charges can be found to hold. So he's not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For lack of evidence, the accused was acquitted for the criminal offence he has been charged with. Okay. Now, with the permission of the Court, I would like to make a brief quotation from this judgement in order to be able to ask you the next question. The incrimination, the charge is as follows, that he participated: "... in the aggression against BiH and violation of the rules of the International Law, regulation of the Article 3, paragraph 1, count a), and the Article 147 IV Geneva Convention of the protection of the civilians in the times of war, and rule of the Article 53 and Article 85 ..." of the Additional Protocol "... on the protection of the victims of international armed conflicts, 1. That he participated, in the period from the beginning of April to September 1992, as a member of the inner leadership group of the terrorist SDS," that's the Serbian Democratic Party, "and Serbian paramilitaries in the Municipality of Hadzici, Binjezevo, and Lower Hadzici, in planning, organising and performing the attack and occupation of the area, in the prosecution of the Bosnian Muslim population, and their deportation to concentration camps and prisons ..." and then 18 Bosniak Muslims are listed, those people who he treated in this manner. Thereby, he committed the criminal offence "... of war crime against civilians (article 142 of CC SFRJ)" that was adopted. We would be interested only in paragraph 2 of this judgement, and we can see here that the legal qualification in this paragraph, that's actually --

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Item 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: -- item 1, that's the criminal offence of war crimes against civilian population, Article 142. Mr. Ilic, do you have this law with you?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, can you point to us the salient points or the salient elements of this criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, the first thing I would like to say is that the characteristic of the offences from paragraph 16 is that they are based on international law, whether international treaties or conventions, and here we are referring to a convention. As regards Article 142, it actually contains all the acts listed in the Geneva Conventions, and since this is a blanket regulation, we have to refer to a particular convention or protocol. So in item 1, we can see that there are two criminal offences with which this person was charged, an attack on the three villages mentioned here and participating in persecution. So there are two acts, two offences. One would be sufficient for him to be found guilty under Article 142, but there are two offences here, attacking a village and participating in persecution. We can find this, and this is in the Geneva Conventions, Article 147 and Article 85 of the protocol. So there are two alternative offences with which this person has been charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The judgement further states that the accused was acquitted because the Chamber deemed that there was insufficient evidence, that all the elements of the criminal offence have been met.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to tell us, very briefly, what does this judgement consist of?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: You are probably interested in the reasons. We have already mentioned the wording, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How is the evidence presented and evaluated?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, the grounds discuss the disposition, so in this case, in the case of an acquittal, the court has the important duty of assessing all the evidence presented. Under our law, there are no strict rules. There are no established rules as to which piece of evidence has more or less weight, so that in each specific case, the trial chamber has to consider all the evidence presented and reach a conclusion. We call that the free assessment of evidence. This is a second logical analysis, and then all the evidence is considered individually and in connection with the other evidence. In this case, 47 witnesses were heard with respect to the two charges. Fifteen were examined at the main trial, and the others had their witness statements read with their agreement. On the basis of this, the court reached its decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have to make this as brief as possible. Please have a look at page 7 of the statement of reasons in this first instance judgement. That's page 6 in the English translation. The court states the reasons why it deemed that there had been insufficient evidence, so I would not want to quote this, to save some time. Could you please comment on this very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: The court has reached its legal conclusion that the accused did not commit the criminal offence. This is not quite properly expressed. The witnesses could not have mentioned direct premeditation because the witnesses wouldn't know about this. The wording is a bit clumsy, but the essence is correct because, on the basis of all the presented evidence, the court concluded that the accused did not commit the crime. When guilt is discussed, then direct premeditation has to be stressed, and they have to say that there was or was no direct premeditation. We have different ways of expressing guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: There is, in this part of the statement of reasons, a sentence that mentions amnesty. Could you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1996, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted the law on amnesty, and it lists all the criminal offences which are subject to amnesty. It was important for the court because the prosecutor went so far as to say that this person was a leader of a group, that he was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, that he wore a uniform, and so on. However, this is immaterial because all the soldiers were amnestied, regardless of whether they were on the Serbian side, the Bosniak side, the Herceg-Bosna side. The amnesty covers all of them. I have this here, but I think it's not necessary to show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, it's not. Let us discuss this premeditation as a form of guilt which you discussed. Can one conclude, on the basis of this judgement, what degree of guilt must be established for criminal responsibility to be there?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: We say that the guilt is the psychological attitude of the perpetrator toward the crime. When we were drawing up the new law, we said that a person is criminally responsible if they are both guilty and mentally competent. The expression means that there are certain forms of guilt, so it can be done with or without premeditation. We have elements of awareness and volition, so the person must be aware and must want to perpetrate the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What does the court require? What has to be established?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: The court had to have proof, if this person had been found guilty, that this person actually -- it's not so important that he took part in the planning, but that this person actually attacked the villages and that he participated in the persecution, and he would -- this would have to be established. It would be insufficient for a witness to say, "Yes, I saw him in a group of soldiers." He would have to say, "I saw him there and there, he was dressed like this, it was this and this time of day." So there would have to be proof, and the person would have to be aware of what he was doing and have the volition to do it, and that would be premeditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness and the parties and the Chamber to be shown the second instance judgement of the supreme court, and we will have a few brief comments about that, and I hope that we will conclude before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D32/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this judgement, and then we could comment on it. Can you really, very briefly, tell us, what did the supreme court decide as regards the first instance judgement, and on whose appeal did it rule?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: There were two charges here, two criminal offences. You are asking me only about the first one, and the supreme court, which is the appellate court of the high court in Sarajevo upheld the decision of the high court in Sarajevo of the 6th of March, 1997, number K8196, with reference to the criminal act of a war crime against the civilian population, which means that they upheld the verdict of not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this is now a final judgement?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a final judgement, and there are no extraordinary legal remedies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You saw the judgements; did the supreme court, when dealing with the appeal, did it consider this only as regards the appeal?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: The supreme court is always an appellate court, and ex officio, it has to monitor whether there has been a miscarriage of justice. The court considered the facts and the procedure, and the court concentrated on whether the facts had been properly established. All the evidence was presented, but perhaps the court might have reached the wrong conclusion, so the supreme court, as the appellate court, has to consider the appeal and explain its reasons, on page 2. In the estimation of the supreme court, everything was done properly and there were not many contradictory witness statements, so the court did not have to clarify possible contradictions. All the witnesses analysed by the court of first instance were reconsidered, and a conclusion was reached to the effect that the appeal was without grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the statement of reasons in this judgement; that's page 2, in both the Bosnian and English versions. It says here -- that's the last paragraph -- however, it only ensues from their testimonies --

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: On page 2, you mean the fifth paragraph? You mean it does not follow from their statements? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, can you just look at this portion.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is it, because the presumption of innocence always holds until guilt is proved, and the court is commenting on this. So it only ensues from the testimony, but it doesn't ensue that he committed the criminal offences, and the court is not interested in the fact that other paramilitary units arrived, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the basis of this statement of reasons -- and I will not be bothering you any more -- what would be the conclusion, would the conclusion be that the court seeks to establish such evidence, what acts, what kinds of evidence should be presented to the court for the allegation of prosecution to be established as guilty?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: According to our law on criminal procedure, there is no evidence which has more weight than other evidence. It depends on the specific situation, the particular situation. In this case, we had witnesses; witnesses are the most frequent kind of evidence, but the least reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that would have to be established?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: So some of these witnesses had to say,"Yes, on such-and-such a day so-and-so came with other people, attacked us, drove us out of our homes, took us to a concentration camp," and so on. Then he would be found guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So in other words, there has to be a specific act; and do you also have to establish the form of guilt of that person?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everyone is responsible for what he has done with premeditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, respecting your request, I have no further questions for this witness, and I would like to thank Mr. Ilic and ask for the Court's indulgence to admit into evidence Defence Exhibits D31 and 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? They are admitted into evidence. Thank you so much indeed, Counsel Krajina, for complying with our request. We will now take a 30-minute break, the only break today, because we will finish at 1.00, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: By the Prosecution? Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. I will just briefly mention to you the scope of the cross-examination I wish to engage in. It will be very brief in any event, but essentially it is not arising out of the areas that have already been covered. Having said that, I do feel it is appropriate, on the basis it is my understanding that the Chamber will always deal with matters of relevance, however, whether or not they are strictly within the scope of the initial direct examination, and I do so on the basis that this is an expert witness on matters judicial and that issues of sentencing do tend to form part of the body of a the work of a Chamber prior to final determination on the facts, and therefore this might be a positive step to ask just a few questions on the theories of sentencing. If that meets with your approval, subject to my friends' comments, I would proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to ask certain questions of this witness in cross-examination, but you immediately addressed the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't see you. All right. So if Mr. Blaxill does not mind, we will first of all listen to Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, if the Prosecutor wishes to ask questions, I have no objection to him being first, but I would just like to remind you that I wished to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask questions regarding legal matters, as the Prosecutor has said, and since this is a blanket provision based on international conventions, I would like to ask you something about the judicial practice, because we ourselves were given the task of providing this Tribunal with our understanding of certain legal terms, so if we as attorneys were asked to do so, it will not be superfluous if you do it, because it can only assist us if you give us your definition of particular legal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in your practice, or in your experience as a judge, you have come across the concept of persecution, and does it differ from persecuting?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Before I came here, I went through the cases that we have dealt with in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I am interested only in the legal side. Is there a distinction between persecution and persecuting?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: In the 13 cases, I did not have the detailed cases, I -- case files, I had just the judgements. But if you ask me now, specifically, I would say that these are two distinct terms, persecution, persecuting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, in your opinion, what is the distinction?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, only if you look at it purely in grammatical terms, but that would be the same kind of legal allegation, but grammatically speaking, these are not the same. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, persecuting is a continuous form, so if I understood it rightly, persecuting lasts a certain time, and persecution can be a one-time act?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you explain what you think is -- what you consider to be persecuting?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, you perhaps -- with the better of looking at some commentaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The commentaries that existed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia said very little about persecuting, and they do not satisfy the requirements of the Defence or of this Tribunal, I believe. So could you please tell us, as an experienced lawyer, what you understand by the term "persecuting"? I am referring to the actions. What actions committed in real life could be subsumed under the concept of persecuting?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a blanket provision. As we have already said, in Article 147, you would not find anything. Then I would refer to the Geneva Convention and see what was defined there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You wouldn't find much more there.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, I would find something more, but if you asked for my opinion on the term of persecuting, that would mean that specifically in the case of this judgement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We're not talking about a specific judgement but about the legal term of persecuting. What, in your opinion as an experienced judge and attorney, should be subsumed under the blanket term of "persecuting"? What actions?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia, in some villages, we had the villages being cleansed. You will not find that anywhere, cleansing, cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness make pauses between answers.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: You can deem that cleansing is also considered as persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit, because it's hard for the interpreters to follow you. I speak fast, and you speak even faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So let us go back to the concept of persecuting. What would have to happen in actual life for someone to be responsible for the act of persecuting?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, that would mean that in a situation of an armed conflict or a state of war, because a war crime could only be committed in the state of war and during an armed conflict, that a group of soldiers or certain persons that have been charged with it would carry out certain acts that could be construed as persecution: Driving people out of their homes, maltreatment of some sort. I cannot now describe that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Can persecuting be perpetrated in other ways, for example, blowing up shops?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Those would be acts of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. But through discrimination?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, discrimination, definitely. You remind me, and I will then give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to hear something from you.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, I can discuss -- this has to do with case law. We did not deal with many cases of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Then we will not go into it any further, but you said that persecuting is a protracted activity. What about persecution?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, as you said yourself, and I accept your opinion, persecution would be a one-off event. You come to a village and you cleanse it in one day, everybody driven out of their homes. For instance, you can see that now in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have not fully managed to achieve what I wanted to, but I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. I see that nobody else is prepared to cross-examine from Defence counsel. Mr. Blaxill, it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Judge Ilic, good morning to you, sir. My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecution team here at the Office of the Prosecutor. I would, in fact, like to move on to just a few brief questions in your expert capacity relating to sentencing practice in war crimes matters in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sir, could you give me, firstly, what are the general parameters, the minimum and maximum type of sentence, that may be given in the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a case of persecution, the war crime of persecution?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: From the 28th of November, 1998, we have a new law in force which envisages at least a five-year imprisonment or long-term imprisonment. Before that, we had the death penalty, which has been abolished. So it's a minimum of five years, and the maximum sentence is long-term imprisonment, that means from 20 to 40 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What, sir, would be the parameter for sentencing practice where there are instances of murders charged as and convicted as war crimes?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards the war crime against civilian population, there are quite a few modalities or acts. If we were to enumerate them, there would be at least 20 of them. Some are minor acts to more serious acts such as murder. Only one such act is sufficient for the conviction. If there are more, however, then the sentence would be more severe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you, in fact, able at this time to quote to us any specific examples of perhaps a person who has been convicted of a war crime perhaps involving an unlawful killing or murder and what kind of sentencing considerations were applied to that?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: If the President would agree to it, I have information regarding 13 judgements reached by the supreme court, and I can give you some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If Their Honours are content with that, perhaps as briefly as you can -- if you just perhaps take a selection from that of, perhaps, six or eight of those of different types. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Of the 13 judgements, the supreme court acting as the appellate court upheld only two. In six or seven cases, the sentences were commuted, and in three cases, the case was returned for retrial. Now let me check if we have murder here. Murder in a camp. It's a case involving a certain person not to be identified, XY. The minimum sentence envisaged by the law was five years and the maximum was death penalty which was commuted to 20 years. In another case, the sentence was commuted to 15 years in prison. That involved a murder committed in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have any specific examples which do cover the concept of persecution within those judgements or do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: No. I just made a note of the conviction and the sentence, so this is just very bare essentials. I did not dwell on it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, what are the specific considerations that the court takes into account by way of, in fact, mitigation of sentences? What issues do they look at which may mitigate the penalty downwards?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, we have some substantial provisions regarding the purpose to be achieved with the sentence and mitigating and aggravating circumstances. In accordance with the presence of those circumstances, then we are seeking to achieve a just sentence between those two extremes, the minimum and the maximum. If there are extremely mitigating circumstances, then a sentence can be mitigated even below the lowest threshold. That's the practice; that's the case law, because the supreme court creates the sentencing policy. So in case of extremely mitigating circumstances, the sentence can be even lower than the legally prescribed minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you say to me what type of things might form such mitigating circumstances in the eyes of the court and perhaps what elements might equally be aggravating elements to be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, there are circumstances which can be seen both as aggravating and as mitigating. If somebody stole something to feed his family and if he took something in order to gamble it away, this fact would be taken as an aggravating circumstance. But what are mitigating circumstances? Because all this is irrelevant in our case. First of all, we have to take into consideration whether this person has already committed such acts, whether he is a recurrent offender. Then what are his general circumstances? What is his behaviour like? Is he prone to criminal behaviour? So on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are there any specific matters that you are aware of that the courts take into account in relation to allegations of war crimes? Are there any things very specific to that sort of issue, either aggravating or, indeed, mitigating?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
