utterances.text: Well, yes, hypothetically speaking, what I would take as a mitigating circumstance, if it were to be established that the criminal offence has been committed, a mitigating circumstance would be, if you compare it to other prisoners, that this person behaved in a better way, treated the prisoners better, that he offered them coffee, cigarettes, so on and so forth. I already said about the fact that that person has no previous criminal record, and also you have to take into account his way of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What about in the war crimes context things that the courts might deem to be aggravating circumstances which might, thus, increase the penalty?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Well, aggravating circumstances -- well, we do not have to -- we mustn’t confuse them with the qualifications, the elements required for a criminal offence. If you were to establish that this person was really very persistent in this kind of behaviour that is culpable, that would be an aggravating circumstance. If he were a guard in the camp, and then if you had several such acts charged in the alternative -- it is really hard for me to speak hypothetically because in different situations, I could give you different answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm much obliged for your assistance. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's the end of the cross-examination by the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Krajina, do you intend to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: President Ilic, I would like to take advantage of the presence here with us of a most distinguished judge from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so I would like to ask you a few questions which, however, are not strictly related to the notion of persecution, we are clear about this notion as set out in the two judgements you commented upon, but these are more general questions. Before, however, I ask you these two questions, may I ask you whether the Court could receive from you the text of the 13 judgements you mentioned before, because they would be of great importance and relevance for us for sentencing, generally speaking, not only in this case. We have already collected quite a few judgements from the former Yugoslavia, I think about 30 from other areas, Belgrade, Zagreb, Sarajevo, and so on, and probably our collection of cases, which is of great importance to us for sentencing purposes, does not include the judgements you mentioned. If you decide, through Krajina, to send them to us, they could be sent in the original language. Of course, if names may not be mentioned, you could simply black out the relevant names. We would be most obliged to you. Let me move on to the general question. I would like to have your comments on one provision of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, which probably has been taken up in the new codes, in the codes adopted in the areas or parts of the former Yugoslavia. I'm referring to Article 23 of the old Criminal Code which was probably applicable in '92 or '90/'91. I will read slowly from the English translation which might not be absolutely accurate. Article 23 provides as follows: "Anybody creating --" I see that probably you have the original text.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: "Anybody creating or making use of an organisation, gang, cabal, group, or any other association with a purpose of perpetrating criminal offences shall be punished for all criminal offences resulting from the criminal design of these associations as if he himself has committed those crimes." Now, would you require premeditation also for the person who has not committed a particular crime but is held here responsible under this provision for the mere fact of participating in a criminal organisation having the purpose of perpetrating criminal offences? Let us leave aside the question of persecution. Of course, this provision clearly applies to any crime, I mean, even an ordinary crime, murder and so on, regardless of an armed conflict. It's a very general provision. I think we can find a similar provision in most European Criminal Codes or even in the case law of the U.K. or the U.S.A. To put it differently, with regard to the case of the person who is held responsible, although he or she has not committed a crime, what sort of actus reus and mens rea would be required for him to be held responsible for the notion under this criminal association or group or whatever?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: I understand the question fully, but I would like to tell you something before I attempt to answer. I have it as Article 26. It is entitled "The criminal responsibility of organisers of criminal organisations." When we carried out the new codification of the Criminal Code, this article was left out, so it no longer is contained in the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, precisely for the reasons that you spoke about. Since we here have incitement and aiding, and we have this criminal organisation and participation therein as a form of being an accomplice, if somebody incited somebody, the actual person who committed the crime, if he was considered an accomplice, from the very text of this provision, it can be seen that this person is responsible for the acts of other people. So we do not talk about direct premeditation. Perhaps we could talk about possible premeditation. Because we wanted to keep that in mind, the issue of guilt, we have left this provision out. It does not exist anymore. The forms of being an accomplice, we have it as aiding and as incitement. These are the only two forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When was it left out? You said that this was a new Criminal Code. When was this new code adopted?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: The 28th of November, 1998, that's when the law came into force. We all know that no law can apply retractably, only milder provisions can be applied because this cannot be considered as milder, since it would include those persons who could not be held responsible otherwise under this culpability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean, of course, that only facts occurring after the 28th of November, 1998 could be covered by the new provision, whereas the old provision, applicable until the 28th of November, 1998, would be applicable. So 23 would be applicable to facts occurring before November of '98; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: No, it would not be applicable. I don't think it that it could be applied because the interim provisions state that once this law enters into force, the previous law ceases to be valid. When this law enters into force, the criminal provisions related to the application thereof are no longer valid. Since this provision is not longer contained here, we could not apply it to events that happened in 1992 and 1993. The only case when something could be applied retroactively is if this is less severe, the new law is less severe. In this case, some person could be charged with organising a criminal organisation which is not contained in this law at all. Maybe you were confused because you applied the principle that the laws that were in effect when a person committed the crime should apply, but I don't think that it applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now give you a case, to ask you how -- again, it's not about persecution. It's a general case, actually, not a figment of my imagination, but which occurred in December of '44, the Second World War. I'd like to see how you, as a distinguished judge from Bosnia-Herzegovina, generally speaking, would deal with such a case, what sort of legal reaction you would have to it. It was in December of '44. Three British airmen were captured by the Germans in a town, Essen. That's why this famous case is called "the Essen lynching case." They were brought to detention units, and from there, the German captain gave to an escort instructions to take the prisoners to the nearest luftwaffe unit for interrogation, the unit of the air forces for interrogation. This order was given out to the escort from the steps of the barracks in a loud voice so that the crowd, a crowd of German civilians, which had gathered could hear and would know exactly what was going to take place. Now, this captain ordered the escort not to interfere in any way with the crowd if they should molest the prisoners. The escort took the three people down the road to take them to their particular unit where they would have been interrogated. On their way to the road, a mob gathered, and the three British airmen were murdered. Some were kicked; some were wounded, beaten up, and so on, by various civilians. The evidence was very clear. It's not a question of evidence. Let us assume that the evidence was as found by the court, and I would assume that this was the right approach by the British court. It was a British military court sitting in Germany in 1945. Some civilians were found guilty because every one of them had, in one form or another, taken part in the ill-treatment which eventually led to the death of the victims, though none of the accused had been exactly proved that they had individually shot or given the blows which caused the death. The captain was sentenced to death, as well as one of the civilians, and one of the escorts was sentenced to terms of imprisonment. In this case, you have mob violence and, of course, I wonder whether you could say that the captain could be found guilty because of premeditation of murder. He was found guilty of murder. Would you approach this case in a different way, based on your own legal training and the basic notions of Yugoslav criminal law or criminal law of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I can see that one can approach this case in a different way, but I would like to know from you how you would deal with this case if you were to sit in judgement on a similar event, on events occurring in this way, or a similar pattern of events.

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: The question is -- well, I can't say "complicated," but interesting. First of all, I would like to say it all depends on the circumstances and the time when it took place because, you see, in Bosnia, the courts would act differently in '93 or in '97 or in '98 because of the difference in the circumstances. However, legality always obtains, but in '93 and in '99, the circumstances are very different. At the time this captain was tried, it was probably very soon after the war. If he were being tried today, it might have been quite different. You see, Dinko Sakic is being tried in Croatia today, and the public attitude to this is different than it would have been right after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I want to know, based on your legal knowledge, your experience, regardless of time, you are an independent judge --

utterances.speaker: VJENCESLAV ILIC
utterances.text: I would not have sentenced him to death. I would certainly not have sentenced him to death. First, his premeditation, he did not have to know how the mob would behave. He might have thought they were just going to beat them up. We can't say that it was direct premeditation, because it's purely hypothetical how the crowd would behave. So I would have to know that he had at least five or six people in the crowd who he knew were going to kill those people. That would have been premeditation. We are not sure, as things stand. So everyone is responsible for what they wanted to happen in their premeditation. This captain was certainly irresponsible and should have been punished, but to be quite honest, I would never have sentenced him to death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there is no -- there are no questions. President Ilic, thank you so much indeed for giving testimony here in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, shall we move on to your next witness, Number Two?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My colleague, Mr. Par, will examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Drmic. I would like you to introduce yourself to the Court, to say your name, date of birth, place of birth, and your profession.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Drmic. I was born on the 12th of January, 1963, in Travnik. By occupation I'm an electronics engineer. I currently live in Vitez. I am employed -- I am self-employed. I have a company that provides accounting services to other enterprises, and also I create software.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In 1993, can you tell us where you were employed and what jobs you performed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1993, the first two months, I worked in a company that I had worked for a couple of years. In the first two months, since the production plummeted due to the war which had already erupted, and the personnel started leaving the company, so in early March, I was laid off, just as my colleagues were. Then sometime in mid-March I was mobilised into the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So since then and throughout 1993, you were in the command of the Vitez Brigade; what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of the financial service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this meant, specifically, what your tasks were, what your duties were in the command? What in fact was the job of the chief of the financial service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in mid-March. I was personally called by the commander of the brigade, Mario Cerkez, since I was familiar with information technology, to assist them at the brigade. I think that the chief of financial service was probably the only post that was vacated at the time, and that's so that I could be employed at the Vitez Brigade, because in the Vitez Brigade at that time there was no post that would include the tasks that I was supposed to carry out. Later on, when I joined the guards brigade, which was formed later, at the brigade staff, there was a post of the assistant for -- adviser for information technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell the Court specifically what your job consisted in. You were at this post; could you tell us what you did, exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Right at the beginning, I kept records of the personnel in the field. Then I created a programme, a computer programme, that would allow me to make a data base of these people, because at that time, before the war broke out the active personnel in the Vitez Brigade, 200 to 300 people, they were deployed on guard duty facing Serbian forces near Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just a moment, please; could we pause there. When you say the "active" part, you are talking about the soldiers who had contracts, salaries; professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the active servicemen had to sign a contract with the Minister, and they were supposed to receive salary for their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I understood you rightly, it was your task to keep a record of these people, in fact to take care of the payroll?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you do anything else, did you draw up any other kinds of lists which you entered into your computer programs containing information and particulars about these people in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the war broke out, my job was more to assist (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you tell us the post of (redacted) in the command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What did you assist her with, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: In the formation of the brigades, making lists, and the payrolls of the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question was, who delivered this information to you? Was it (redacted) And who delivered it to her, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: The data was sent to us from the field. Those were the data that were the most credible. But right at the beginning, we did not receive this data in the form that we had to receive it in, because the brigade was not structured right at the beginning. I don't think that it was established in the proper manner until the very end of 1993, because it was a continuous process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: To conclude, these lists were given to you; it was your job to enter them into the computer. Did you compare this data with the situation in the field? In other words, did you verify it? How correct were those data?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely the task that I had, to collate the data, because the data coming to us from the field were very imprecise. I think that it was done very quickly, and the data were not complete. We did not have a father's name -- or names of the fathers of some the members of the units, dates of birth, so that we could not establish with any precision the identity of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, the question -- when I asked about the precision of this data, did you have any cases regarding the payroll when the number of men reported to be in the units changed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Well, with the first salaries, we did not have any problems before the outbreak of the war, but sometime in late 1993, in December, an order was issued from the command, higher command, that there would be some problems with the payroll, because the members of the HVO in Herzegovina had already received their salaries, and there were some rumours that we could also get paid. Then, when the commanders of the units in the field were asked to provide updated lists, the situation changed radically in comparison to the situation that we had so far, so we collated the data several times so as to be able to know precisely where people were, whether they were indeed employed in the unit, in order to have the final number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When you say "radically different," it changed radically, are you referring only to the number of persons, or the particulars, the details of these persons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Both the number of persons and their personal details. The number usually increased by several percentage points, but so did the accuracy of the information. Sometimes I had people in my records who did not exist at all. Because perhaps the commander in the field asked, "what is this guy's name? He is not here," and then the answer was wrong. And we just had this piece of paper that we had to use, and later on it would turn out that this person did not exist at all, or one person would be entered in the records in two places by mistake with different dates of birth, and if we did not have the father's name, we could not ascertain whether or not that was indeed the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us now if you know Vlatko Kupreskic personally, and if you do, where you met him.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I know Vlatko Kupreskic personally. We met for the first time in this company where we worked together before the war. For a while we worked in the same building, so we saw each other from time to time, and we would exchange the time of day. We never entered into any discussions. I saw him once during the war, and after the war, we collaborated in the business, in our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We shall come to that later. When you were working on the register of men liable for military service, was Vlatko Kupreskic registered as fit for military service, or not fit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I don't know when Vlatko was registered in our records, but he was registered as unfit for military service, and next to his name there was no unit, no military unit listed. So he did not belong to any of the military units. We just had his name in our files, just as a we had the names of various old people or young people or women.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So what was the marking next to his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I had a system of marks, for instance, the letter "P" would mark a man who had died, and next to his name was the mark "N," which meant "unfit for military service."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Drmic, how it was established at that time that someone was unfit for military service. Was there a medical board, did any documents have to be presented? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: In my work with (redacted), for somebody to be declared unfit for military service, an opinion of the military medical board was required, because that board declared whether somebody was fit or unfit on the basis of the medical evidence presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly when you say that (redacted) did that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: That was the job of (redacted), who was in (redacted) . And since I was in the same (redacted), I assisted her in her work, and I simply remember some things. I did not want to remember this particularly, but it happened so that I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: To be more precise, (redacted) sat in the same room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Since Vlatko Kupreskic was registered as unfit for military service, was he liable to conscription or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: According to the regulations, persons unfit for military service were not to be mobilised or conscripted, but in our situation things were a bit different it was not as in normal armies, countries or wars. There were periods when nobody could claim that they were unfit for military service. Everybody had to be involved in some cases when the enemy attacked, everybody had to make their contribution regardless of their inability but in accordance with their abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So, although formerly he was not liable to mobilisation, there were some situations when he could not claim that, he could not refer to that. Do you know that such a special situation concerning Vlatko Kupreskic actually occurred? In other words, do you know that he was mobilised in spite of the fact that he was not liable for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do know. On that occasion when I saw him during the war, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic was brought to our office, to (redacted) and myself, he was in civilian clothes, and he was brought in by two persons in uniforms, I think these were military policemen, but I can't recall that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us when this happened? Can we discover the time? And could you tell the Court what happened, who said what, what was done, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly when it was, because at that time I did not commit such things to my memory. But as far as I can remember, sometime in September, when the enemy attack against our positions was at its fiercest. I think it was at this period when a lot of personnel were no longer able to fight because they were either killed or wounded. Then the military police attempted to bring in those persons who had not been mobilised, who were unfit for military service, to bring them in by force and to mobilise them. As far as I can remember it was sometime in the second half of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Since you said that you don't remember the exact date, could you tell us how far off you think you might be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Well, a month, or two months at the most, but not more than that. I think that maybe Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic might know that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I wanted you to tell us what happened. You were sitting in the office; who else was there, what was said, what happened when these two persons in uniform brought Vlatko in? Do you remember the details? Do you remember what happened, who said what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I remember that very well. (redacted) (redacted) and myself were in the office when two uniformed persons brought Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic into the room, and they told her, "Here is another one for you to assign." Then they left the room, and (redacted) then talked to Vlatko. He showed her some papers indicating that he was unfit. I did not pay much attention to that, because I had a job to do myself. After this conversation, which lasted maybe five or ten minutes, Vlatko left the room, and (redacted) (redacted) looked at me in a strange way, in a meaningful way. I looked at her questioningly. It's as if she was trying to tell me something, but I couldn't understand what it was. She then said, perhaps angrily, "You see," she said, "what these are doing to me. They are bringing me" -- and they I looked at her questioningly; I didn't know what was going on. She said, "They are bringing to me people who are unfit, and they want me to assign them to units, and I cannot do anything with them." I looked at her in confusion; what was going on? I didn't know. She said, "Well, Vlatko has a pacemaker." I was surprised, myself, because I did not know that fact, although I had known him from before. Then (redacted), since she did assign him to a unit, she gave me those papers, and I entered the data into our computer, and he was -- Mr. Kupreskic, Vlatko, was registered as having been assigned to the medical platoon at the brigade level. So it wasn't at the level of the lower units, but he was assigned as a driver of the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So he was assigned to be a driver in the medical platoon, and he had to report for duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This has left an impression on me, and that's why I remember it so clearly, as if it happened yesterday, although five or six years have passed. If it had been somebody else, I maybe would not remember it, but I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I intend to show a certificate, Prosecution Exhibit 329. I would like to ask the usher to show P329, the exhibit, to the witness. Maybe we can speed things up by putting it on the ELMO. If I'm not wrong, it's P329, Mr. Terrier? I would like to ask the usher to give the witness the Croatian text so that he can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Drmic, I have shown you this before. Could you look at it now. It says in this certificate that Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised from the 16th of April, '93, to the 15th of January, '96, as an assistant commander for the medical corps. You said that he was mobilised only in September or around September, so could you explain or comment on the data in this certificate, and could you account for the discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with these certificates because at that time virtually every member of the Vitez Brigade got one, and they were mostly issued in the course of 1996. At the Federation level, a decision was made that all members of the BH army and of the HVO were entitled to certain salaries, arrears of salaries which had not been paid; but due to the lack of money, they were supposed to receive some securities, some shares, which would then be used by them. When lists were made for those shares, you had to have a certificate from your unit which would then be used to determine the time that you spent in a certain unit. As for the date, the initial date, the 16th of April, in our records in the Vitez Brigade, we did not have this date for Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, just as we didn't have it for other people who were not mobilised at the beginning of the war or before the war. For this final date here, the 15th of January, 1996, I don't know whether that is correct or not, because I was involved with Vlatko Kupreskic in business, and throughout 1995, I saw him virtually every day. He was a businessman wearing civilian clothes. So I don't know anything about that. As for the post, assistant commander for medical corps, I could not comment on that, because I know that (redacted) assigned him as a driver in the medical corps. Whether he was promoted later to a higher post or a higher rank, I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing his post, assistant commander for the medical corps, can you tell us whether at that time there was a medical corps within the Vitez Brigade or whether there was a unit, a medical unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, well, virtually in the first few months of the war, the medical platoon existed only in theory. In practice, no personnel were assigned to it. I know that because I talked about it to the chief of medical service, Dr. Bosko Pavlic. One day we met in the corridor and we spoke informally. That was after the beginning of the war. He told me, "These guys are crazy." Nobody heard our conversation. I didn't know what he meant, and I asked him to explain. He said the war -- "There's a war going on, and the medical corps has not been established. We do not have the vehicles, we do not have stretchers, nothing." So this duty that's listed here, assistant commander of the medical corps, in this initial stage, is highly questionable, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a certificate like this? Did you personally, as a member of the brigade, get this kind of certificate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and so does virtually every other member of the Vitez Brigade. And one other thing that I can say with regard to the certificate, I think that no member of the Vitez Brigade has a date that will be before 16th of -- after the 16th of April. That's the earliest date, although some people were mobilised months later. I think that the reason for this was to help people so that they get more money, the salaries that were owed to them. So that's why I have two certificates, in effect, because I joined the brigade two times. In early 1994 I was reassigned to the guards brigade, and then when I was discharged from the guards brigade, I was again assigned to the Vitez Brigade, so I have two such certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Drmic, I will now show you a report by the Defence Department, and this is Prosecution Exhibit -- I would like to ask the usher to give the witness the Croatian text. It's P335. Since I have shown you this document before, you know what it is about and everybody in this courtroom knows what it refers to, could you please say whether you know what the data here is based on and who provided this data to the department? Was it provided by the people from the Vitez Brigade? Do you know how the data for this report was collected? Who delivered it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this document was issued by the defence department in Vitez, and as we know, this is an institution that keeps the record or records of people fit for military service and which has to mobilise those people in the case of war and to assign them to their units. In the course of these events, however, in the spring of 1993, in Vitez, in fact, the process was reversed. The Vitez Brigade conducted mobilisations rather than the defence department, and that's why we had our own lists and we submitted those lists to the defence department which then returned the lists to us, proforma as if it was them who mobilised them. This is a document prepared by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I can stop you for a moment. This is the reason I posed the question. We saw from your testimony that you kept the records of this personnel and then delivered this information, and you did the mobilisation. Did you personally deliver this information to the department? What is the relation between this data and the data you had in your records?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: In the first 10 to 15 days, we did not have much data. We only started collecting data after that 10-day or 15-day period. Some information came to us directly from the front lines and some from the defence department. This data did not come from our records but from the defence department. I don't know who this report was submitted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know how they came by this information or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they got this information or who drafted this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at number 107 where it says that Vlatko Kupreskic is a person who was mobilised on the 16th of April, 1993. Could you please say, since this differs from your records, how he came to be on this list? Do you know how his name could have come to be on this list with this date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I don't have any specific information as to how he appeared on this list, you will have to ask the person who drew it up, but I am familiar, to a certain extent, with this list because I received a number of lists throughout the war. Whether I received this particular list, I don't know, but what it says at the end, "duty officers, military police assigned to Darko," I'm familiar with it. It's as if I had seen something like that, as if I had held this in my hands. It probably was submitted by the department of defence to (redacted) and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Finally, you see that certain documents indicate that Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised on the 16th of April, 1993. Do you still maintain that this is not the case, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: We put all the records in our computer. As the brigade became better established, each member was assigned to a certain unit. Those units had codes which I assigned. The first one was the number of the battalion, company, and squad. So for each member, we had a code indicating which unit he belonged to. In many cases, though, people did not have that code next to their names and we did not know whether they belonged to the brigade at all and whether they had a record somewhere. In such cases, we always talked to the platoon and company commanders to discuss that, to see whether they are, indeed, members of their units, whether we could count on them or not. In this manner, Vlatko did not have a code next to his name. He was designated as unfit for military service up until that time when he was mobilised into the medical corps. In addition, when I read this report, when you showed it to me, I saw that from the 16th of April until the 20th of April, this is the date when this list was drawn up, and here are some lists, in my view, it means that these people, the people on this list were not mobilised on the 15th of April. They were not members of the Vitez Brigade as of the date when the conflict broke out. In my opinion, it probably happened four or five days after the outbreak of the war when the enemy forces launched a serious attack on Vitez. That would be the 21st and the 22nd of April. That is when the mobilisation began in earnest because some people were engaged in town to collect people and to send them to collect weapons. They did not have uniforms at that time at all. Also, looking at this list, I know most of these people. My conclusion is that these are mostly people from the lower part, as we say, the eastern part of Vitez which was bordering on Zenica, whereas people in the areas bordering on Travnik, Zabrdze, and Kruscica were not on those lists, nor were they mobilised. Most of them were from the lower part bordering on Zenica and from the town of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drmic. Your Honours, I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there is no other Defence counsel waiting to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drmic. I'm Franck Terrier. I'm one of the trial attorneys for the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you a few questions following the testimony you just gave. A few moments ago, you said that the first serious attack against Vitez was launched on the 22nd of April, 1993. What happened prior to the 22nd of April? Nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: It started on the 16th of April. That was when the war actually started in our part of the world. During the first few days, there was gunfire; there were detonations. I did not know exactly what was going on. Even though I was a member of the Vitez Brigade, I was simply not informed. When I came to work -- it started on Friday. I turned up for work on Monday. I was a little surprised, and I found that the person on duty -- the person on duty had a notebook, and he always received information from the field about who had been killed or wounded. Around the 21st or the 22nd, we had more frequent reports of casualties because people started -- there were fewer people on the front lines, so there was a need to have more personnel. I think the first serious attack on Vitez happened only on the 22nd when there were the most casualties during the first days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In your recollection, what happened on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, the war started. I woke up in the morning. I was awakened by detonations and the sound of guns and mortar launches. I didn't know what was going on. I was called by a man working for the defence office. He was a neighbour of mine. He asked me to come downstairs and to come up with the rest of the tenants so that we could discuss what to do and perhaps have guard duty at the entrance to our building. During these discussions, people came bearing rumours. Someone probably received a telephone call from someone, and in the evening of that day or perhaps the next day, I learned that something terrible had happened in the village of Ahmici, that there had been many civilian victims, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Drmic, where did you live exactly at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I lived in the very centre of town, in the building where the town pharmacy is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That morning of the 16th of April, as you said yourself, the war had started. That was your expression. Did you right away get in touch with your unit, the commander of the brigade in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not get in touch. I expected that someone would come and tell me what was going on, that someone would call me. I was surprised, and I simply thought it was best for me to stay at home with my wife and child. Later in the course of that day, I don't know exactly what time it was, my neighbour asked me to come downstairs and to meet with him and other neighbours in front of the building so that we could organise guard duty. In fact, I spent the first three days there, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. I expected that someone would call me or tell me what was going on, but it was only on Monday when I went to the commander of the brigade, and they asked me, "Where have you been so far?" And I didn't know what to say because I thought they would call me, tell me what was going on, because the war had been going on for three days, and no one had told me. That day, I met (redacted) and she had done the same as me and only turned up for work on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: A few moments ago, you said that on that evening, the 16th of April, or the day afterwards, you had learned that something terrible had happened in the village of Ahmici. Can you be more specific and tell us how you have come to learn about those events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I heard that from some neighbours of mine who are tenants in the same building. Whether they had heard about it by telephone or whether some members of some units had arrived -- for example, I had a neighbour who was a member of the civilian police, and in the evening when he came home, he would drop in. He confirmed this, and he said that what we had already heard was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On that day, on the 16th of April, probably in the evening or late afternoon, you heard from two different sources that something terrible had happened in Ahmici on that same day. You learned it from your neighbours and one member of the civilian police; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, from one of my neighbours, I don't remember exactly who, and in the evening, when this policeman was going home from the police station in the town, we asked him, "Is it true," and he confirmed that it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you be as precise as possible as to the information you received then as to what had happened in Ahmici, particularly what you heard from the policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: We were told that several houses had been set on fire, I can't say the number, but that several women and children had been killed, that there had even been bodies on the road, that sometimes a body would be hanging out of a house window. We wanted to make use of our acquaintance with this policeman to find out if this was true or whether it was just a rumour that had been made up by someone, and he confirmed that something unexpected, something terrible had really happened, something that was unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In your mind, from that day, and in the minds of the people who you talked to, since you're talking about several women and children killed, I mean, there is no doubt to the fact that it is a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear to me because, in my opinion, women and children should be left out of wartime operations. Because this could have happened to my own wife and to my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you wonder, on that day or the following days, or did you receive information, confidential information regarding the perpetrators of that crime and the circumstances in which that crime was perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Of course, I wondered what could have happened in people's minds for something like this to happen, but in my opinion, these people who did that, after that, they must have realised what they had done. For all of us in Vitez, to this day, it is shrouded in mystery, and, in fact, nobody knows who actually did it, because it was probably in the interest of the perpetrators not to have it talked about and for people not to know about it. Perhaps during the war, it was dangerous, in a way, to know too much and to ask too many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in the course of the questions by Mr. Par, two documents were shown to you. One is marked 321, which is an exhibit from the Prosecutor, and the other one is marked 335. The first one is a certificate signed by Colonel Vinac, and the second is a report signed by Marijan Skopljak. Upon a reading of those two official documents, it appears that at the date of the 16th of April, '93, Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised in the HVO. What are the reasons that would lead us not to believe those two documents which match one another?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: This certificate should not be believed because the date, the 16th of April, is on almost everybody's certificate about their mobilisation, although in many cases, this is not true. In my experience, in working with data and the register of personnel, I know that Vlatko Kupreskic was not assigned to a military unit up to the moment when he was actually forcibly brought into the premises of the Vitez Brigade. So I doubt this date and especially the post of assistant commander of the medical corps, because I think he was a driver. After that, I don't know whether he was assigned to a different duty. As regards the second document, it does not show the date of mobilisation for anyone. I think that anyone who is on this list, if they were asked about the dates, they would probably say, "This is not the date." So I doubt this because I think the active part of the Vitez Brigade, which was established before the war, which had uniforms, which had equipment, which had salaries, these were the people who were prepared for the war. Everybody else, especially these people on this list, they were not prepared for the war. In my opinion, these people were forcibly mobilised and did not volunteer, most of them, because I think they did not have equipment. I don't know whether they had weapons. This list drawn up by the defence office shouldn't look like this because when the defence office submits data, a person's name must also be accompanied by the father's name and the date of birth. This looks like a list drawn up by someone stopping people in the street and just saying, "What's your name," and writing it in. I know most of these people. If you saw some of these people, if you saw what they look like, it would be quite clear to you that these people are not fit for military service, that these people simply would not be able to conduct a war, and that this list also includes elderly people and people unfit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you consult that list of names, you will see that across from their names there are particular markings. For instance, there are markings before numbers 24, 85, and 86, and there's a marking also before Number 149. Before number 84, 5, 6, and 7, there is no marking as to the delaying of mobilisation up until the 26th of April, '93.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I don't see any markings in front of the numbers. It's empty on the list I have. But I think that this is not really a mobilisation. In my opinion, this is something superficial. I don't know how some people came to be included in this list. And the comments in the right-hand margin next to the list, such comments were introduced in our records later on, to put a date or a letter or a marker telling us something more about this person, because very often they did not have a date of birth, or the father's name, or their place of residence, because the organisation was such that people went to the defence lines according to the place where they lived. It was very rare for people to be moved from their village somewhere else. I see here that the people from the lower part, as we call it, in the direction of Zenica, I can see this from their names, and they're also from the centre of the town, and people from the other parts of the municipality are not on this list at all because for them, the war had not started yet. For them, it started somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Mr. Witness, given your position at the time, and even from the 16th of April up until the following Monday, you were not in your office, could you describe to us how, from a material point of view, the mobilisation was conducted for the purposes of the war which was starting between the HVO forces and the Muslim forces? So from a material point of view, how did the mobilisation actually take place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I may not understand your question properly. Could you explain what you mean by "material"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I mean what was the work that had to be done in order to inform people, to tell them that they were mobilised? Was it done by telephone, by mail, by sending them messages, and what were the orders given to those people? What was, for instance, possible -- military training that was given to those people, how were they given their military clothing and weapons, you know, this sort of information is what I'd like you to give us now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. People were mostly caught in the streets. If someone left their flat to get supplies for their family or to buy something, and if he was seen by a person who was in charge of mobilisation, and they were people from the special units and people working for the administration department, they would simply catch that person in the street and send them to the warehouse to be issued weapons, to the depot, to issue them weapons, and then they would be taken directly to the defence lines. So that was one of the methods. They were caught in the streets of the town. The second method was, these units would go from house to house, enter the apartments, and look for male members of the family who were fit for military service, and then they would simply take them away, put them in a car and assign them to a defence line. This was the most frequent method of mobilisation in the first days of the war. It was only later, when a month or two had elapsed, when we had established lists, registers, then we -- and we got these lists from the commanders -- then we would send these lists to the defence office and ask them to undertake a legal procedure putting these people at our disposal and delivering their documents to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In fact, if I listen to you, it was by coincidence that people were mobilised after the outbreak of the war? I mean, all it would take was to leave your home to go and buy bread, and all of a sudden you would find yourself on the defence line, on the front line. On the opposite, if you stayed at home, chances were that you would not be mobilised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, unless he was found by the units, and there were situations where people hid under the bed, or that's what I heard later. They would hide so as not to be mobilised and taken to the front line. They were afraid, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you have any specific information regarding the mobilisation of the men who lived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: No. I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You did not say to us at what time those people who were mobilised in the circumstances you explained received weapons, military equipment, and possibly also instructions as to how they were to use those weapons.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: After they were caught, so to speak, or brought in, they were sent to the building where the depot was to be issued with equipment, and without any training and without sufficient weapons, because there were not enough weapons for everyone, they were sent barehanded to the front line simply to swell the numbers, so that if someone was wounded, they could take that person's weapons. Very often people took their hunting rifles with them, or their parents' hunting rifles. This was the solution they found, although it was a bit ridiculous. I know this very well, because my best friend was wounded on the 22nd of April, and he told me about it in the -- he had taken his father's hunting rifle and gone to the front line. He was wounded. He had been shot through the leg, and his nerve was damaged so that his leg is paralysed now. He had this experience. He went there with his father's hunting rifle without a uniform, without anything, and he was wounded very soon, at the very beginning, like many others, because then the hospitals started filling up with wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Witness, tell us about the reserve servicemen of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, all of these people were reserve servicemen, because only the active part at the moment the war started, only they were active servicemen. All the others were reservists, and they were included in the units of the Vitez Brigade or other brigades gradually. Apart from them, there were some elderly people, over 60 or 70 years of age, who contributed in their own way. Most often they would take food to the soldiers at the front line, or in the evening they would patrol their own villages, without weapons, without uniforms, simply so that they would be doing something and not sitting at home. Those younger than 18 did the same, if they wanted to feel they were doing something. There were cases when young men of 15 were killed on the front line, or when walking through the town, because there was frequent shelling, especially of the roads and streets, and there were some women, a number of women who were involved because they cooked food for the soldiers. Almost all of them were later issued with the certificates as if they had been members, and I think they all have this date, the 16th of April, as the initial date. The second date, I don't know what it's based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I get you right, Mr. Witness, what you've just said is that all the members of the Croat community in Bosnia were, one way or the other, mobilised for the war effort as soon as the war started; the elderly were committed as they brought material support -- for instance, sending food. Women were also involved by cooking for the soldiers, and people of age became fighters. And what you've also said, and please correct me if I have misunderstood what you said, is that before the outbreak of the war, men of age to fight were either in a position of activity for military purposes or then they were considered as reservists.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC
utterances.text: I think, if I understand you rightly, that that is correct. But the war started, there were two or three hundred active servicemen. The rest of us were all reservists, as long as there was no war, because each of us has his file in the defence office and is registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Terrier. It's 1.00; do you have many more questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: About 10 to 15 minutes, but that can be put off to tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we shall resume tomorrow. The hearing is adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.
